q: What is the main difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
options: Unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data and supervised learning predicts from labelled data
Unsupervised learning predicts from labelled data and supervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data
Unsupervised learning needs rewards from an environment and supervised learning does not
Unsupervised learning only predicts numbers and supervised learning only predicts classes
explain: Supervised learning learns from input and output pairs to predict outcomes. Unsupervised learning has no labels and looks for patterns or groupings in the data itself.

q: A chemistry dataset describes wines by their measured properties but has no column giving the wine type. Which task is the data suited to?
options: Regression, to predict the wine type as a number
Clustering, to discover whether natural groups of wines exist
Classification, to learn from the known wine type column in the data
Reinforcement learning, to reward the right wine type
explain: With no labels there is nothing to predict in a supervised way, so the sensible task is to look for groups. Classification and regression both need a target column.

q: Which of these are common unsupervised learning methods?
options: Decision trees
Linear regression
K-means
Autoencoders
Principal component analysis
explain: K-means, principal component analysis and autoencoders find structure without labels. Linear regression and decision trees learn from labelled examples.

q: Which statements about clustering are correct?
options: It predicts a continuous number for each new data point
It works without a target variable or predefined categories
It groups points that are close or similar by some measure such as distance
It needs labelled examples of every group before it can start
It can be used as an exploratory tool to find hidden structure
explain: Clustering is similarity based, unsupervised and exploratory. The wrong options describe supervised classification and regression.

q: A shop wants to split its customers into groups by behaviour and preferences so it can tailor its marketing. Which task is this?
options: Market basket analysis using clustering
Regression to forecast next month's sales
Customer segmentation using clustering
Dimensionality reduction of the customer data
explain: Grouping customers by behaviour is segmentation, a clustering task. Market basket analysis looks instead for products bought together.

q: A supermarket wants to discover which products are often bought together. What is this application called?
options: Document clustering
Gene analysis
Customer segmentation
Market basket analysis
explain: Market basket analysis discovers associations between products that appear in the same purchase. Customer segmentation groups the customers themselves.

q: Which list gives the steps of k-means in the correct order?
options: Place centres at random, assign points to the nearest centre, move centres to cluster means, repeat
Assign points to clusters, place centres at random, repeat until all clusters are the same size
Move centres to cluster means, place centres at random, assign points once and stop
Place centres at the data mean, label each point, then train a model on the labels
explain: K-means starts with random centres, assigns each point to the closest centre, moves each centre to the mean of its points, and repeats. It does not stop after one pass or need labels.

q: K-means is run twice on the same data with the same k and returns different clusters. What is the most likely cause?
options: K-means moves the data points themselves a little on every pass it makes through the data
The starting cluster centres were chosen at random and were different each time
K-means randomly changes the number of clusters on each run
The distance measure changes at random from one run to the next
explain: The initial centres are placed at random, so different starting points can lead to different final clusters. The value of k is fixed by the user.
flag: Run to run variation is textbook knowledge. The slide only shows that centres start at random.

q: In k-means, what does it mean to say the algorithm has converged?
options: Every cluster has been given exactly the same number of points as the others
All centres have moved to the overall mean of the dataset
No point changes its cluster membership when the process is repeated
The value of k has reached the number of data points
explain: Convergence is reached when repeating the assign and move steps no longer changes which cluster any point belongs to.

q: Why can you not simply pick the value of k that gives the lowest inertia?
options: Inertia is the same whatever value of k is used, so it cannot compare them
Inertia rises as k grows, so the smallest k would always be chosen
Inertia can only be worked out when k is two, so other values give no result
Inertia keeps falling as k grows, so the lowest value is always the largest k
explain: Inertia keeps falling as more clusters are added, so the lowest value would always point to the largest k. This is why the elbow, where improvement drops sharply, is used to choose k instead of the minimum.
flag: The slide says inertia falls as k rises, the conclusion about not using the minimum is a standard reading.

q: On a plot of inertia against k, which point marks a good choice of k in the elbow method?
options: The point after which the rate of improvement drops drastically
The point where inertia first becomes zero
The point where inertia is at its highest value anywhere on the whole plot
The point where the line is perfectly straight
explain: Adding clusters helps a lot at first, then very little. The bend where this change happens is the elbow, although it can be hard to see.

q: A point has a silhouette value close to 0. What does this say about the point?
options: It is very well clustered and far from other clusters
It lies on the boundary between two clusters
It is the exact centre of its own cluster
It was left out of every cluster by the algorithm
explain: Values near 1 mean a well clustered point and values near 0 mean it sits between clusters. Negative values suggest it may be in the wrong cluster.

q: Which statements about the parts of the silhouette score are correct?
options: The separation term is the average distance to points in the nearest neighbouring cluster
The score ranges from 0 to 100 for each point
The cohesion term is the average distance to other points in the same cluster
The overall score is the largest value found among all the points
A good clustering has small cohesion distances and large separation distances
explain: Cohesion measures tightness within a cluster and separation measures distance to the nearest other cluster. The overall score is the average over all points, and each value lies between minus one and plus one.

q: How is the silhouette score used to choose the number of clusters?
options: Try several values of k and pick the one with the average score closest to minus one
Try several values of k and pick the largest, because more clusters are always better
Try several values of k and pick the one with the highest average score
Try several values of k and pick the one where the score first drops below zero
explain: The best k is the one that maximises the average silhouette score. Too few clusters give low separation and too many give fragmented, unstable clusters.

q: Which clustering method groups points by density and can find clusters of arbitrary shape?
options: K-means
Hierarchical clustering
Gaussian mixture models
DBSCAN
explain: DBSCAN is density based and is good for irregular cluster shapes. K-means favours compact groups around centres.

q: A researcher wants a tree diagram showing how clusters merge or split at different levels. Which method gives this?
options: Hierarchical clustering, which builds a dendrogram
K-means, which builds a dendrogram around centres
DBSCAN, which builds a dendrogram from densities
Principal component analysis, which builds a dendrogram of features
explain: A dendrogram is the tree produced by hierarchical clustering. The other methods do not produce one.

q: Which are benefits of reducing the number of features in a dataset?
options: Data can be plotted in two or three dimensions
The data gains a labelled target column
Faster computation
Less noise and redundancy
Lower risk of overfitting
explain: Fewer features speed things up, remove noise, reduce overfitting and allow plotting. Reducing features never creates labels.

q: What does principal component analysis do to a dataset?
options: It groups the points into a set number of clusters
It projects the data onto directions that capture the greatest variance
It predicts a label for each point from known examples that carry labels
It deletes the points that lie furthest from the mean
explain: Principal component analysis finds new axes, the principal components, along which the data varies most, and projects the data onto them. It is not a clustering or prediction method.

q: How does linear discriminant analysis differ from principal component analysis?
options: It is unsupervised and tries to maximise the total variance kept in the data
It is non-linear and only preserves very local structure
It is supervised and tries to maximise the separation between classes
It is a clustering method that finds density based groups
explain: Linear discriminant analysis uses class labels to separate classes. Principal component analysis uses no labels and keeps variance.

q: In principal component analysis, each eigenvalue of the covariance matrix belongs to one direction in the data. What does a large eigenvalue say about that direction?
options: The direction is noisy, so it should be removed
The direction contains outliers that form a cluster of their own
The direction is the label that the model must predict
The direction captures a large share of the variance in the data
explain: Each eigenvalue shows how much the data varies along its direction, which is what the explained variance ratio is built from. Directions with large eigenvalues are the components worth keeping.
flag: The link from eigenvalue size to explained variance is standard textbook linear algebra, the slides show it only through the explained variance ratio.

q: A dataset has four features. After principal component analysis, the first one or two components explain almost all the variance. What does this suggest?
options: The features overlap a lot, so fewer dimensions can summarise them
The four original features were all completely unrelated to one another
The data must contain exactly one or two natural clusters
The remaining components must be the most important ones
explain: If a few components hold most of the variance, the features overlap heavily, so a low dimensional summary loses little information. It says nothing direct about the number of clusters.
flag: The slide gives the variance figures, the interpretation about redundancy is standard.

q: Which statements about k-means are correct?
options: Each centre is moved to the mean position of its cluster
It needs a labelled target to place the centres
The user chooses the number of clusters k
It always finds clusters of any shape
explain: K-means needs k set in advance and it moves each centre to the mean of its points. It uses no labels and favours compact groups.

q: Which of these are dimensionality reduction methods?
options: Principal component analysis
t-SNE
Linear discriminant analysis
DBSCAN
UMAP
explain: The first four reduce the number of features. DBSCAN is a density based clustering method.

q: Compare supervised and unsupervised learning in terms of the data they use and what they aim to do.
model: Supervised learning uses labelled data, which are input and output pairs, and aims to predict outcomes for new data. Linear regression, decision trees and neural networks are examples. Unsupervised learning uses unlabelled data and aims to find inherent structure or patterns. K-means, principal component analysis and autoencoders are examples. For instance, supervised learning could predict house prices from past sales, while unsupervised learning could group customers by behaviour without any predefined groups.
points: States that supervised learning uses labelled data and unsupervised learning uses unlabelled data
States that supervised learning aims to predict and unsupervised learning aims to find structure
Names a correct algorithm for each
Gives a correct example of each, such as predicting prices and grouping customers

q: Explain what clustering is and give one real application.
model: Clustering is an unsupervised technique that groups similar data points together based on their features, without any labels or target variable. Points that are close under some measure, such as distance, end up in the same cluster. It is used as an exploratory tool to find hidden patterns. A common application is customer segmentation, where a business groups customers by behaviour and preferences so that marketing can be tailored to each group.
points: Says clustering is unsupervised with no labels or target
Explains that similar or close points are grouped together
Describes it as exploratory for finding hidden structure
Gives a valid application such as segmentation

q: Describe how the k-means algorithm works, including when it stops.
model: K-means divides the data into k clusters, where the user chooses k. It first places k centres at random. It then assigns every point to its closest centre and moves each centre to the mean position of the points assigned to it. These two steps repeat. The algorithm stops when no point changes its cluster membership, which is called convergence. Overall it aims to minimise the total squared distance between points and their cluster centres.
points: Says k centres start at random
Describes assigning points to the closest centre
Describes moving each centre to its cluster mean
States that it repeats until membership stops changing
Mentions minimising squared distances

q: Explain how the elbow method helps you choose the number of clusters in k-means.
model: Inertia is the sum of squared distances from each point to its cluster centre, and smaller values mean tighter clusters. Inertia falls as k increases. The elbow method plots inertia against k and looks for the point where the rate of improvement drops sharply. That bend is the elbow and suggests a good value of k, because adding more clusters beyond it gives little benefit. The elbow can be hard to see on some plots, so another measure may be needed.
points: Defines inertia as the sum of squared distances to the cluster centre
Says inertia decreases as k grows
Identifies the elbow as where improvement drops sharply
Notes the elbow can be hard to see

q: Explain what the silhouette score measures and how it is used to choose k.
model: The silhouette score shows how well each point fits its own cluster compared with other clusters. It compares the average distance to points in the same cluster with the average distance to points in the nearest neighbouring cluster. Values run from minus one to plus one. Near plus one means well clustered, near zero means on a boundary and negative means possibly misclassified. To choose k, run k-means for several values, average the score for each and pick the k with the highest average.
points: Describes cohesion within the cluster versus separation from the nearest cluster
States the range from minus one to plus one with meanings
States that the overall score is an average over points
Says the best k maximises the score

q: Compare k-means with DBSCAN and say which suits clusters of irregular shape.
model: K-means groups points around centres by minimising squared distance, and the user must choose k in advance. It tends to find compact, roughly round groups. DBSCAN groups points by density, so it can find clusters of arbitrary shape. For data where the clusters are curved or irregular, DBSCAN is the better choice. K-means is simpler and the most popular method, and it suits compact groups where a sensible k can be found.
points: Describes k-means as centre and distance based with k chosen by the user
Describes DBSCAN as density based
Says DBSCAN finds arbitrary shaped clusters
Gives one situation where each method would be chosen
flag: The point that k-means favours compact round groups is standard knowledge, the slide only says DBSCAN suits arbitrary shapes.

q: Explain what dimensionality reduction is and why it is useful.
model: Dimensionality reduction reduces the number of input features while keeping as much relevant information as possible. It projects the data into a lower dimensional space. This makes high dimensional data easier to visualise, analyse and process, and it helps with the curse of dimensionality. It also speeds up computation, reduces noise and redundancy and lowers the risk of overfitting. Methods include principal component analysis, linear discriminant analysis, t-SNE and UMAP.
points: Says it reduces the number of features while preserving information
Mentions projection into a lower dimensional space
Gives at least two benefits such as speed, noise, overfitting or visualisation
Names a method

q: Describe the main steps of principal component analysis and what the result is used for.
model: First the data is centred by subtracting the mean of each feature. Next the covariance matrix is calculated to show how features vary together. Eigen-decomposition of this matrix gives eigenvectors, which are the principal components, and eigenvalues, which show how much variance each carries. The data is then projected onto the chosen components. Keeping only the first few components gives a smaller summary that keeps most of the variance, which helps visualisation and can be useful before clustering.
points: Mentions centring the data
Mentions the covariance matrix
Says eigenvectors give the components and eigenvalues give the variance
Says the data is projected onto the top components

q: Compare principal component analysis with linear discriminant analysis and with t-SNE.
model: Principal component analysis is unsupervised and linear. It projects data onto the directions of greatest variance. Linear discriminant analysis is supervised, so it uses class labels and tries to maximise the separation between classes. T-SNE is a non-linear method that preserves local structure and is mainly used to visualise data in two or three dimensions. So the choice depends on whether labels exist and whether the aim is to keep variance, separate classes or plot neighbourhoods.
points: Says principal component analysis maximises variance and needs no labels
Says linear discriminant analysis is supervised and separates classes
Says t-SNE is non-linear and preserves local structure for visualisation
